title: Plans and Predictions
overview: Say what is already arranged, what you have decided, and what you only think will happen. Use am, is and are with an -ing word for a fixed arrangement: I am meeting her on Tuesday. Use going to for a decision you have made, and will for a guess. Say why you are doing something with to and a plain verb.
learningPath: The lesson: listen, then say each line.
Words: 28 words for plans, guesses and weather.
Patterns: 3 cards. Read the worked one first.
Reading: two short texts and a travel notice.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, then listen back.
Writing: four tasks. Made-up answers are fine.
Practice: six exercises. Check each one with the answers.
Quiz: 12 questions. Then look at My progress.
lectureScript:
Hello. This is Unit 4.
In this unit you talk about what happens next.
There are three kinds of next. English says each one differently.
The first kind is arranged. You and another person agreed it.
For this, use am, is or are, and the verb with -ing.
I am meeting the doctor on Tuesday.
She is starting her new shift on Monday.
We are not working on Friday.
The -ing form is the same one you use for now.
The time word makes it a plan. On Tuesday. At six. Next week.
Say the time, and nobody thinks you mean now.
Ask it like this. Are you working on Saturday?
The second kind is a decision. You decided it yourself.
For this, use going to.
I am going to phone the office tomorrow.
He is going to postpone the meeting.
Going to also works for a sign you can see.
Look at the sky. It is going to rain.
The third kind is a guess. You do not know.
For a guess, use will.
I think it will be warm on Sunday.
It will probably stop by lunchtime.
Will is short in speech. I'll call you. It'll be fine.
Here is the line between the two.
A decision, or a sign in front of you? Going to.
Only a guess in your head? Will.
Now the words for how sure you are.
Probably is nearly sure. Possibly and perhaps are less sure.
Put probably after will. It will probably rain.
Put perhaps at the front. Perhaps it will rain.
Likely comes after it is. It is likely to rain.
Now the last pattern, and it is short.
To say why you are doing something, use to and the plain verb.
I am going early to get a seat.
I am writing it in my diary to remember it.
No comma. No for. Just to, then the verb.
Ask why, and answer with to.
Why are you going early? To get a seat.
Now some words you will use all unit.
A diary and a schedule hold your times.
An invitation asks you to come. A reminder tells you again.
Available means free. Spare means not used.
If a plan moves later, you postpone it. That is a delay.
If you take the other thing, you say instead.
If two people change days with each other, they swap.
And the weather. A forecast says what the weather will do.
Drizzle is small, light rain. A breeze is a light wind.
Thunder is the loud noise. Lightning is the bright light.
Fog is thick cloud on the ground.
Frost is white ice on a cold morning.
A flood is water on land that is usually dry.
That is the whole unit.
Arranged: am, is, are and an -ing word.
Decided: going to. Guessed: will.
And to plus a plain verb, for why.
Now do the three cards, then the practice.
Say every line out loud. Your voice is part of the lesson.

words.meaning: A small book, or an app, where you write your days and your times.
words.example: I write every appointment in my diary.
practice: My diary says I am seeing the doctor at ten.
Is Friday free in your diary?
She keeps her diary on her phone.
I looked in my diary before I said yes.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor what people write in a diary for one working week. Use made-up days, not your own.

words.meaning: A list of times that says when each thing happens.
words.example: The schedule for Monday starts at seven.
practice: The bus schedule changes at the weekend.
My schedule is full until Thursday.
Can you send me the schedule for next week?
The new schedule gives me one spare hour.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the difference between a diary and a schedule. Then say one sentence with each.

words.meaning: A message that asks you to come to something.
words.example: The invitation came by email.
practice: I sent the invitation last week, and she said yes.
Have you answered the invitation yet?
The invitation says six o'clock on Saturday.
Thank you for the invitation.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for two polite lines to answer an invitation: one yes and one no.

words.meaning: A short message that tells you again, so you do not forget.
words.example: My phone sends me a reminder an hour before.
practice: Set a reminder for Tuesday at nine.
The office sent a reminder about the appointment.
I need a reminder, or I will forget.
This note is a reminder to buy bread.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor when a reminder is useful in a busy week. Then say one sentence with reminder.

words.meaning: Free, and able to come or to be used.
words.example: I am available on Friday morning.
practice: Are you available at four?
No seats are available on that train.
The doctor is not available until Monday.
I am available after six, but not before.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for a polite way to say you are not free. Then say two sentences with available.

words.meaning: A plan that two people have agreed together.
words.example: We have an arrangement for Tuesday at ten.
practice: The arrangement is that she comes to me.
Is the arrangement still for six o'clock?
I must change our arrangement for Friday.
We made the arrangement last week.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the difference between a plan and an arrangement. Then say one sentence with arrangement.

words.meaning: To send a message on to another person.
words.example: I will forward the invitation to you.
practice: Can you forward me the schedule?
She forwarded the email to the office.
Forward it to me, and I will answer.
I forwarded the reminder to my colleague.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor what you write at the top when you forward a message. Use made-up names.

words.meaning: Extra, and not being used.
words.example: I have a spare hour on Wednesday.
practice: Wednesday is my spare day.
Keep a spare key in your bag.
Have you got a spare pen?
There is one spare seat at the front.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three things it is useful to keep a spare one of.

words.meaning: Nearly sure. You think yes, but you do not know.
words.example: It will probably rain this afternoon.
practice: She will probably arrive before six.
The bus is probably late again.
I will probably work on Saturday.
That is probably the best day for us.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor where probably goes in a sentence with will. Then say three sentences about next week.

words.meaning: It can happen, but you think it is not very likely.
words.example: It will possibly be foggy in the morning.
practice: I can possibly come at four, but I am not sure.
The road is possibly closed after the storm.
She will possibly swap days with me.
Possibly, but I must look at my diary first.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor which is stronger: probably or possibly. Then say one sentence with each.

words.meaning: Maybe. It usually goes at the front of the sentence.
words.example: Perhaps it will be dry tomorrow.
practice: Perhaps we can meet on Thursday instead.
Perhaps the train is delayed.
Perhaps I will take a taxi.
Perhaps, but I need to check first.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three sentences that start with perhaps. Then say them back to it.

words.meaning: Something that will probably happen.
words.example: Frost is likely tonight.
practice: It is likely to rain before lunch.
A delay is likely after twelve.
Snow is not likely in the afternoon.
Which day is the most likely for a flood?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor how to use likely after it is. Then say two sentences about the weather.

words.meaning: To say now what you think will happen later.
words.example: Nobody can predict the weather for next month.
practice: The forecast predicts thunder after four.
Can you predict how long the delay will be?
I predicted rain, and I was right.
It is hard to predict a busy day.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the difference between predict and guess. Then say one sentence with each.

words.meaning: To think that something will come, or will happen.
words.example: I expect a delay after twelve.
practice: We expect twenty people at the meeting.
Do not expect an answer before Monday.
She expects the bus at half past six.
I did not expect the invitation.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for two sentences with expect: one about a person, one about the weather.

words.meaning: To say an answer when you do not know it.
words.example: Guess how long the queue is.
practice: I can only guess the time of the next bus.
Do not guess. Look at the schedule.
She guessed the answer, and she was right.
My guess is that it will be foggy.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to say a weather word. You guess what it means, then you both swap over.

words.meaning: To think about something you do not know, and want to know.
words.example: I wonder what the weather will do.
practice: I wonder if the meeting is still on Friday.
She wondered why the train was late.
I often wonder how they predict a storm.
I wonder whether he got my invitation.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three questions that start with I wonder. Then answer all three yourself.

words.meaning: Small, light rain that falls slowly.
words.example: There is drizzle all morning in the forecast.
practice: It is only drizzle, so I am walking.
The drizzle stopped after an hour.
Drizzle is wet, but it is not heavy rain.
Take a coat. There will probably be drizzle.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the difference between drizzle and heavy rain. Then say one sentence with drizzle.

words.meaning: A light wind that is pleasant.
words.example: There is a warm breeze from the sea.
practice: A cold breeze came through the open window.
A light breeze makes a hot day easier.
I like a breeze in a warm room.
The forecast says a breeze in the evening.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor when a breeze becomes a wind. Then say two sentences with breeze.

words.meaning: The loud noise you hear in a storm.
words.example: We heard thunder after four o'clock.
practice: There will be thunder this afternoon.
The thunder woke me at two in the morning.
Thunder is loud, but it cannot hurt you.
After the thunder, the rain got heavier.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor which one you see first in a storm, and which one you hear. Then say one sentence with thunder.

words.meaning: The sudden bright light in the sky in a storm.
words.example: We saw lightning over the sea.
practice: Lightning is bright, and it lasts one moment.
Do not stand under a tree in lightning.
The forecast expects lightning after three.
There was lightning, and then a very loud noise.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for two safe things to do in a storm with lightning.

words.meaning: Thick cloud on the ground, so you cannot see far.
words.example: There is fog on the road this morning.
practice: The fog is thick, so the bus is slow.
Drivers go slowly in fog.
The fog was gone at about ten.
Fog is likely by the river tonight.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor what a driver does in thick fog. Then say one sentence with fog.

words.meaning: Thin white ice on the ground on a very cold morning.
words.example: There was frost on the car at seven.
practice: Frost is likely tonight, so drive slowly.
The frost stayed until nine o'clock.
Plants do not like a hard frost.
The forecast predicts frost before Friday.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor what frost does to a road in the early morning. Then say one sentence with frost.

words.meaning: What people say the weather will do.
words.example: The forecast for Thursday is not good.
practice: The forecast says drizzle, then thunder.
I look at the forecast before I leave.
The forecast was wrong again.
A forecast for next week is often wrong.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor which words in a forecast mean it is not sure. Then say two of them in sentences.

words.meaning: Water that covers land that is usually dry.
words.example: The flood closed the low road.
practice: After three days of rain, there was a flood.
A flood warning is open for the river.
The flood stopped the buses for a day.
Floods are more likely in a wet month.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor what a flood warning tells people to do. Then say one sentence with flood.

words.meaning: Extra time you wait before something happens.
words.example: There is a delay of twenty minutes.
practice: The fog caused a long delay.
Expect a delay after twelve.
Sorry for the delay. I am on the next bus.
A short delay is not a problem for me.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for a polite message to send when you have a delay of ten minutes.

words.meaning: To move something to a later time or day.
words.example: We are going to postpone the meeting.
practice: Can we postpone it until Friday?
The storm postponed the whole trip.
She postponed her appointment twice.
I would rather postpone than cancel.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for the difference between postpone and cancel. Then say one sentence with each.

words.meaning: In the place of the first thing.
words.example: The bus is full, so I am walking instead.
practice: Let us meet on Thursday instead.
There is no coffee, so I will have tea instead.
Take bus 12 instead, and you will be quicker.
She could not come, so her brother came instead.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for two sentences with instead: one about food, one about travel.

words.meaning: To give one thing and take another, with a person.
words.example: Can we swap days next week?
practice: I swapped my Saturday for his Monday.
She wants to swap seats with me.
Let us swap, and we will both be happy.
We swap shifts when one of us is not available.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for a polite way to ask a colleague to swap a day with you.

grammar.title: Meeting her on Tuesday: it is arranged
grammar.explanation:
Use am, is or are with the verb and -ing for a plan you have already arranged.
Another person knows about it too.
I am meeting the doctor on Tuesday.
Say the time, and nobody thinks you mean now.
We are not working on Friday.
grammar.rule:
Arranged, with the time said:
I am meeting the doctor on Tuesday.
You are starting on Monday.
He is coming at six.
We are travelling next week.
They are moving in May.

Not arranged:
I am not working on Friday.
She is not coming to the meeting.

Ask:
Are you working on Saturday?
Yes, I am. No, I am not.
What are you doing on Thursday?

The same words mean now when no time is said:
I am meeting the doctor. (now, in this room)
I am meeting the doctor on Tuesday. (arranged)
grammar.workedExample:
I ___ ___ my sister on Sunday. (see)
1. The person is I, so use am.
2. See takes -ing: see, seeing.
3. Put am, then seeing.
4. I am seeing my sister on Sunday.
5. Check: is there a time? Yes, on Sunday.
6. So this is a plan, not now. Good.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to drop am, is or are.
No: I meeting her on Tuesday.
Yes: I am meeting her on Tuesday.
It is also easy to leave the time out.
I am meeting her. That sounds like now.
Add the day, and it becomes a plan.
grammar.tip: Three parts: am, is or are, then the -ing word, then the day.
grammar.practice:
Write am, is or are, and the verb with -ing.
1. I ___ ___ my sister on Sunday. (see)
2. We ___ ___ at six on Friday. (leave)
3. She ___ ___ the invitation today. (send)
4. They ___ ___ to the market in the morning. (go)
5. He ___ not ___ on Thursday. (work)
6. ___ you ___ on Saturday? (come)
7. The new nurse ___ ___ on Monday. (start)
8. I ___ ___ for a friend on Friday. (cook)
grammar.answers:
1. am seeing  2. are leaving  3. is sending  4. are going  5. is, working  6. Are, coming  7. is starting  8. am cooking
Am goes with I. Is goes with he, she and it. Are goes with you, we and they.
Wrong on 5? In a not sentence, not sits between is and the -ing word.
Wrong on 6? In a question the be word comes first, and it takes a capital letter.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read the card again and do it twice.

grammar.title: Going to for a decision, will for a guess
grammar.explanation:
Going to is for a plan you have decided, and for a sign you can see.
I am going to phone the office tomorrow.
Look at the sky. It is going to rain.
Will is for a guess. You do not know.
I think it will be warm on Sunday.
grammar.rule:
Decided already:
I am going to phone the office.
She is going to postpone it.
We are going to swap days.

A sign in front of you:
Look at the sky. It is going to rain.
The river is very high. It is going to flood.

A guess in your head:
I think it will be dry tomorrow.
It will probably stop by lunchtime.
Perhaps it will be foggy.

Short forms:
I'll call you. It'll be fine. It won't rain.

Where the sure words go:
It will probably rain.
Perhaps it will rain.
It is likely to rain.
grammar.workedExample:
Look at that black cloud. It ___ rain.
1. Is this a decision? No.
2. Is there a sign you can see? Yes, the black cloud.
3. A sign takes going to.
4. It is going to rain.
5. Now take the sign away: I think it ___ rain tomorrow.
6. No sign and no decision, so it is a guess.
7. I think it will rain tomorrow.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to drop the be word in going to.
No: I going to phone the office.
Yes: I am going to phone the office.
It is also easy to use will for a decision you already made.
No: I will phone the office tomorrow. It is in my diary.
Yes: I am going to phone the office tomorrow.
grammar.tip: Decided, or a sign you can see? going to. Only in your head? will.
grammar.practice:
Write going to or will. The first line tells you which.
1. I have decided. I ___ postpone the meeting.
2. I think it ___ be warm on Sunday.
3. Look at that black cloud. It ___ rain.
4. Nobody knows. The forecast ___ probably be wrong.
5. We have agreed a day. We ___ swap Monday and Friday.
6. The river is very high. It ___ flood.
7. Perhaps it ___ snow tonight.
8. My bag is packed. I ___ leave at six.
grammar.answers:
1. am going to postpone  2. will be  3. is going to rain  4. will probably be  5. are going to swap  6. is going to flood  7. will snow  8. am going to leave
Decided already, or a sign in front of you? going to, with am, is or are.
Only a guess in your head? will, with no am, is or are.
Wrong on 4? Probably sits between will and the verb.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read the card again and do it twice.

grammar.title: Going early to get a seat: the reason after to
grammar.explanation:
To say why you are doing something, use to and the plain verb.
I am going early to get a seat.
Put it straight after the first part, with no comma.
Ask why, and answer with to.
Why are you going early? To get a seat.
grammar.rule:
Why? Answer with to and a plain verb:
I am going early to get a seat.
I am phoning to change my appointment.
She is writing it in her diary to remember it.
We are leaving at six to miss the traffic.

The verb after to never changes:
to get, to change, to remember, to ask
Not: to getting. Not: to gets.

The short answer to a why question:
Why are you going early?
To get a seat.

Two ways to say the same thing:
I am going early to get a seat.
I am going early because I want a seat.
grammar.workedExample:
Join these two: I am leaving at six. I want to miss the traffic.
1. The second part says why.
2. Take out I want, and keep to.
3. That leaves: to miss the traffic.
4. Put it after the first part, with no comma.
5. I am leaving at six to miss the traffic.
6. Check: to, then a plain verb? Yes, to miss.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to add -ing after to.
No: I am going early to getting a seat.
Yes: I am going early to get a seat.
It is also easy to put for in front of the verb.
No: I am going early for get a seat.
Yes: I am going early to get a seat.
grammar.tip: Ask why. If the answer starts with to and a plain verb, it is right.
grammar.practice:
Answer each question. Start your answer with To.
1. Why are you going early? (get a seat)
2. Why is she phoning the office? (change her appointment)
3. Why are you writing it in your diary? (remember it)
4. Why are they leaving at six? (miss the traffic)
5. Why do you set a reminder? (arrive on time)
6. Why are you looking at the forecast? (plan Saturday)
7. Why is he taking a coat? (stay dry)
8. Why are we swapping days? (help each other)
grammar.answers:
1. To get a seat.  2. To change her appointment.  3. To remember it.  4. To miss the traffic.  5. To arrive on time.  6. To plan Saturday.  7. To stay dry.  8. To help each other.
Every answer starts with a capital T and ends with a full stop.
The word after to is plain: get, change, remember. Never getting, never gets.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read the card again and do it twice.

readings.title: My week, and what the weather will do
readings.setting: Sunday evening, looking at the week ahead.
readings.passage:
My week is busy, and most of it is already arranged.
On Monday I am meeting a friend after work.
On Tuesday I am seeing the doctor at ten.
I have written both in my diary, to remember them.
Wednesday is my spare day. Nothing is arranged.
I am going to clean the kitchen and answer my messages.
Thursday is the hard one. I am starting at seven, not at nine.
I am going early to get a seat on the bus.
The forecast for Thursday is not good.
Drizzle in the morning, then thunder in the afternoon.
It will probably be wet all day.
Perhaps I will take a taxi instead.
On Friday a friend is coming for dinner.
I sent the invitation last week, and she said yes.
I am buying the food on Thursday evening, to save time.
I think Friday will be the best day of the week.

readings.title: How sure is a forecast?
readings.setting: A short explanation of weather forecasts.
readings.passage:
A forecast tells you what the weather will probably do.
It is a guess, but it is not a wild guess.
People measure the air, the cloud and the wind.
Then a machine works out what is likely.
A forecast for tomorrow is usually right.
A forecast for next week is often wrong.
Read the words, not only the picture.
Some words are strong. Rain is coming. There will be thunder and lightning.
Some words are soft. It will possibly be foggy. Frost is likely in the morning.
Soft words mean the forecast is not sure.
Numbers help too. Eight in ten means the rain is nearly certain.
Two in ten means it will probably stay dry.
A warning is different. A flood warning is not a guess about your day.
It is a message to act on, so look at the times and the places on it.
And make a plan you can change. Weather moves, so a second idea is worth having.

readings.title: Saturday travel notice: bus 7
readings.setting: A notice at a bus stop, on the Friday before.
readings.passage:
SATURDAY 14 - TRAVEL NOTICE

BUS 7
Normal times until 11 in the morning.
From 11, one bus every hour, not every twenty minutes.
Reason: work on the road by the bridge.

WEATHER
The forecast is heavy rain from 12 to 4.
A flood warning is open for the low road by the river.
Bus 7 will not use the low road while the warning is open.

WHAT TO DO
Going to the market? Leave before 11.
Going to the hospital? Take bus 12 instead. It runs every twenty minutes all day.
Carrying a heavy bag? The stop by the bridge is closed. Use the stop by the library.

DELAYS
Expect a delay of ten to twenty minutes after 12.
We are sorry. We cannot say more than that today.

NEXT SATURDAY
Normal times. The road work finishes on Friday.

comprehension.q: Which two things are already arranged for Monday and Tuesday?
comprehension.a: Meeting a friend on Monday, and seeing the doctor on Tuesday.
comprehension.why: The text says: On Monday I am meeting a friend after work. On Tuesday I am seeing the doctor at ten.

comprehension.q: How sure is the speaker that Thursday will be wet?
comprehension.why: The speaker says it will probably be wet, and probably means nearly sure. Perhaps I will take a taxi shows there is still a choice.

comprehension.q: Why is the speaker buying the food on Thursday evening?
comprehension.a: To save time before the dinner on Friday.
comprehension.why: The text says: I am buying the food on Thursday evening, to save time. The dinner is on Friday.

comprehension.q: Which forecast is usually right: tomorrow's or next week's?
comprehension.why: The text says a forecast for tomorrow is usually right, and one for next week is often wrong.

comprehension.q: The text calls some forecast words soft. What does soft mean here?
comprehension.a: The forecast is not sure about them.
comprehension.why: The text gives possibly and likely as soft words, and then says soft words mean the forecast is not sure.

comprehension.q: A forecast says it will possibly be foggy. Should you change your whole day?
comprehension.a: No. Possibly is a soft word, so the forecast is not sure.
comprehension.why: The text says soft words mean the forecast is not sure. It also says a warning, not a soft word, is the thing to act on.

comprehension.q: You are going to the hospital on Saturday afternoon. Which bus do you take, and how long do you wait?
comprehension.a: Bus 12, and it comes every twenty minutes.
comprehension.why: The notice says to take bus 12 for the hospital, and that bus 12 runs every twenty minutes all day.

comprehension.q: You want the market, and you do not want to wait an hour. When do you leave?
comprehension.why: Bus 7 keeps normal times until 11. From 11 there is only one bus an hour.

comprehension.q: Why will bus 7 not use the low road by the river?
comprehension.a: Because a flood warning is open for it.
comprehension.why: The notice says a flood warning is open for the low road. It also says that bus 7 will not use that road.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — It is already arranged
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each line.
I am meeting the doctor on Tuesday.
She is starting at seven on Monday.
We are swapping days next week.
I am not working on Friday.
Are you coming on Saturday?
Tap the mic. Say the five lines.
Tap the mic again. Listen back.
Check: do you say am, is or are before every -ing word?
speaking.tutor: Say the five lines to the tutor. Then say three arrangements for your own week. Made-up days are fine.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Decided, or a guess
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each line.
I am going to phone the office tomorrow.
Look at the sky. It is going to rain.
I think it will be dry on Sunday.
It will probably stop by lunchtime.
Perhaps it will be foggy.
Tap the mic. Say the five lines.
Tap the mic again. Listen back.
Check: the going to lines have am or is in them. The will lines do not.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say a short situation. Answer with going to or with will, and ask it which one fits and why.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Why are you going early?
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each question, then its answer.
Why are you going early? To get a seat.
Why are you phoning? To change my appointment.
Why are you leaving at six? To miss the traffic.
Why are you taking a coat? To stay dry.
Tap the mic. Say all four pairs.
Tap the mic again. Listen back.
Check: does every answer start with to and a plain verb?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for four more why questions about a busy week. Answer each one with To and a plain verb.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Fixing a time
speaking.instructions:
Two people fix a time. You say both parts.
You: Are you available on Thursday morning?
Other: No, I am working until one. Are you free on Friday?
You: Friday is better. What time are you finishing?
Other: At four. Shall we say half past four?
You: Half past four is fine. I am writing it in my diary now.
Other: Good. I will send you a reminder.
Tap the mic. Say all six lines, one after the other.
Tap the mic again. Listen back.
Check: three questions, and two voices you can tell apart.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be the other person. Fix a time to meet next week, and ask it at least three questions.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — What do you think will happen?
speaking.instructions:
Say what you think, and say how sure you are.
I think it will probably rain tomorrow.
Possibly, but I am not sure.
Perhaps the bus will be late again.
Frost is likely tonight.
I expect a delay after twelve.
Tap the mic. Say the five lines.
Then say three more about next week. Made-up answers are fine.
Tap the mic again. Listen back.
Check: does every sentence say how sure you are?
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor three things you think will happen next week. Ask it which of the three sounds the most sure.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — One minute about next week
speaking.instructions:
Talk for one minute about next week.
Say two things that are already arranged.
Say one thing you have decided, with going to.
Say one guess about the weather, with will.
Say one sentence with to, to give a reason.
Everything can be made up.
Tap the mic. Talk for one minute.
Tap the mic again. Listen back.
Check: two -ing arrangements, one going to, one will, one to sentence.
speaking.tutor: Talk to the tutor for one minute. Then ask it to count your going to sentences and your will sentences.

writing.title: Writing 1 — My week, already arranged
writing.prompt:
Write 4 sentences about arrangements for next week.
Every sentence names a day or a time.
Your week can be made up.
writing.model:
On Monday I am meeting a friend after work.
On Tuesday I am seeing the doctor at ten.
We are swapping days on Wednesday.
I am not working on Friday.
writing.criteria:
4 sentences.
Every sentence has am, is or are and a verb with -ing.
Every sentence names a day or a time.
1 sentence with not.
A capital letter and a full stop in each.
writing.support:
Copy the model. Change the day and the last two or three words only.
Then check each -ing word against the list on Card 1.
writing.extension: Turn one of your sentences into a question: Are you working on Friday?

writing.title: Writing 2 — Decided, and guessed
writing.prompt:
Write 4 sentences about next Saturday.
2 decisions, with going to. 2 guesses, with will.
Everything can be made up.
writing.model:
I am going to clean the kitchen in the morning.
I am going to buy the food before twelve.
I think it will be dry until lunchtime.
It will probably rain in the afternoon.
writing.criteria:
4 sentences.
2 with am or is and going to. 2 with will.
1 sure word: probably, possibly or perhaps.
A capital letter and a full stop in each.
writing.support:
Write the two going to sentences first. Both start I am going to.
Then write the two guesses. Both start I think it will, or It will.
writing.extension: Add one sentence about a sign you can see: Look at the sky. It is going to rain.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Why I am doing it
writing.prompt:
Write 4 sentences. Each one says what you are doing and why.
Use to and a plain verb for the why part.
Everything can be made up.
writing.model:
I am leaving at six to miss the traffic.
I am going early to get a seat.
I am setting a reminder to arrive on time.
I am writing it in my diary to remember it.
writing.criteria:
4 sentences.
Every sentence has to and a plain verb.
No comma before to.
4 different verbs after to.
A capital letter and a full stop in each.
writing.support:
Write the first part only: I am leaving at six.
Then ask yourself why, and add to and one plain verb.
writing.extension: Write two why questions, and answer each one with To and a plain verb.

writing.title: Writing 4 — A message to move an arrangement
writing.prompt:
Plan, write and check a message of 6 sentences.
You cannot come to an arrangement, so you ask to move it.
Plan 5 lines: the old day, the reason, two new days, and what you think.
Write: say what was arranged, say you cannot come, and say why.
Then offer two new days, and say what you think will happen.
Check twice: once for am, is and are, once for the full stops.
Use a made-up name and a made-up day.
writing.model:
We are meeting on Thursday at four.
I am very sorry, but I cannot come.
I am working until six that day to cover a shift.
Are you available on Friday or on Monday?
Friday is better for me, because I have a spare hour.
I think Monday will be busy for both of us.
writing.criteria:
A plan of 5 lines.
6 sentences.
1 sentence with am, is or are and an -ing word.
1 sentence with to and a plain verb.
1 question that asks if the other person is available.
1 sentence with I think and will.
A capital letter and a full stop in each.
writing.support:
Do the plan first: five short lines, one for each part.
Then write one sentence for each line of the plan.
Use Writing 1 and Writing 3 as your models.
writing.extension: Read your message out loud and record it. Listen back, and mark any sentence with no verb in it.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Arranged: the -ing plan
activities.instructions:
Write am, is or are, and the verb with -ing.
1. I ___ ___ the doctor on Tuesday. (see)
2. She ___ ___ her new shift on Monday. (start)
3. We ___ ___ days next week. (swap)
4. They ___ ___ to the market on Saturday. (go)
5. He ___ not ___ on Friday. (work)
6. ___ you ___ the invitation today? (send)
7. My friend ___ ___ for dinner at seven. (come)
8. I ___ ___ the office at four. (phone)
activities.answers:
1. am seeing  2. is starting  3. are swapping  4. are going  5. is, working  6. Are, sending  7. is coming  8. am phoning
Am goes with I. Is goes with he, she and it. Are goes with you, we and they.
Wrong on 3? Swap doubles the p: swapping. Work does not double: working.
Wrong on 6? A question starts with the be word, and it takes a capital letter.
7 or 8 right: good, and this outcome is met. 6 or less: read Card 1 again and do it twice.
activities.solo: Write your answers on paper. Then check each one with the key, and count the right ones.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Going to, or will?
activities.instructions:
Write going to or will. The first line tells you which.
1. I have decided. I ___ phone the office tomorrow.
2. I think it ___ be dry on Sunday.
3. Look at the river. It ___ flood.
4. We have agreed a date. We ___ postpone the meeting.
5. Perhaps it ___ snow tonight.
6. Look at that black cloud. There ___ be thunder.
7. I do not know, but I think she ___ say yes.
8. My bag is packed. I ___ leave at six.
9. Nobody knows. The forecast ___ probably be wrong.
10. The queue is very long. We ___ be late.
activities.answers:
1. am going to phone  2. will be  3. is going to flood  4. are going to postpone  5. will snow  6. is going to be  7. will say  8. am going to leave  9. will probably be  10. are going to be
Decided already, or a sign in front of you? going to, with am, is or are.
Only a guess in your head? will, with no am, is or are.
Wrong on 6 or 10? Look at and the queue is very long are both signs you can see.
8 or more of 10: good, and this outcome is met.
6 or 7: read Card 2 again and do the ones you got wrong.
5 or less: do Card 2 and its practice again first.
activities.solo: Write the ten answers on paper, then check them with the key. Say each right sentence out loud once.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Join the two parts with to
activities.instructions:
Join the two parts. Use to and a plain verb. Write one sentence.
1. I am going early. I want to get a seat.
2. I am phoning the office. I want to change my appointment.
3. She is writing it in her diary. She wants to remember it.
4. We are leaving at six. We want to miss the traffic.
5. I am taking a coat. I want to stay dry.
6. He is setting a reminder. He wants to arrive on time.
7. They are swapping days. They want to help each other.
8. I am looking at the forecast. I want to plan Saturday.
activities.answers:
1. I am going early to get a seat.
2. I am phoning the office to change my appointment.
3. She is writing it in her diary to remember it.
4. We are leaving at six to miss the traffic.
5. I am taking a coat to stay dry.
6. He is setting a reminder to arrive on time.
7. They are swapping days to help each other.
8. I am looking at the forecast to plan Saturday.
Take out I want or she wants, and keep to and the verb. No comma.
Wrong anywhere? Check that the word after to has no -s and no -ing.
7 or 8 right: good, and this outcome is met. 6 or less: read Card 3 again and do it twice.
activities.solo: Write all eight on paper. Then check the word after to against the key, one line at a time.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Match the word to its meaning
activities.instructions:
Match the word to its meaning. Write the number and the letter.
1. diary   2. schedule   3. invitation   4. reminder   5. available
6. spare   7. forecast   8. drizzle   9. postpone   10. swap
a) small, light rain
b) free, and able to come
c) a message that asks you to come
d) what people say the weather will do
e) to move something to a later time
f) a book or an app where you write your days
g) extra, and not being used
h) a short message that tells you again
i) a list of times that says when each thing happens
j) to give one thing and take another, with a person
activities.answers:
1 f, 2 i, 3 c, 4 h, 5 b, 6 g, 7 d, 8 a, 9 e, 10 j
Diary and schedule are the easy two to mix up. A diary is the book; a schedule is the list of times.
Postpone and swap are the other pair. You postpone a time; you swap with a person.
9 or 10 right: good. 8 or less: read the word groups again and do it once more.
activities.solo: Cover the meanings with your hand and say each word first. Then match, and check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Find it in the travel notice
activities.instructions:
Read the Saturday travel notice again. Write short answers.
1. How often does bus 7 run after 11 in the morning?
2. Why is bus 7 slower that day?
3. What time does the heavy rain start?
4. Which road will bus 7 not use, and why?
5. You are going to the hospital in the afternoon. Which bus do you take?
6. How often does bus 12 run?
7. Which stop is closed, and which one do you use instead?
8. Are the times the same on the next Saturday?
activities.answers:
1. One bus every hour.
2. There is work on the road by the bridge.
3. Twelve o'clock.
4. The low road by the river, because a flood warning is open.
5. Bus 12.
6. Every twenty minutes, all day.
7. The stop by the bridge is closed. Use the stop by the library.
8. Yes. Next Saturday has normal times, because the road work finishes on Friday.
Wrong on 4 or 8? Both answers need two lines of the notice, not one.
7 or 8 right: good, and this outcome is met. 6 or less: read the notice again and point at the line for each answer.
activities.solo: Answer all eight from the notice, then check the key. For any you got wrong, point at the line that holds the answer.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Find the one mistake
activities.instructions:
Every sentence has one mistake. Write it again, the right way.
1. I meeting the doctor on Tuesday.
2. Look at the sky. It will going to rain.
3. I am going early for get a seat.
4. She is going to postponing the meeting.
5. It will probably to rain.
6. I am phoning to changing my appointment.
7. We are swap days next week.
8. He is start his new shift on Monday.
activities.answers:
1. I am meeting the doctor on Tuesday.
2. Look at the sky. It is going to rain.
3. I am going early to get a seat.
4. She is going to postpone the meeting.
5. It will probably rain.
6. I am phoning to change my appointment.
7. We are swapping days next week.
8. He is starting his new shift on Monday.
1, 7 and 8 are about am, is, are and the -ing word.
2, 4 and 5 are about the verb after going to and after will: keep it plain.
3 and 6 are about to and the plain verb that follows it.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: do Cards 1, 2 and 3 again, one a day.
activities.solo: Copy each sentence, then write your new one under it. Check with the key, and mark which card each mistake came from.

quizzes.q: I ___ meeting the doctor on Tuesday.
quizzes.why: I takes am. Is goes with he, she and it. Are goes with you, we and they. Be is the plain form, and it cannot stand here.

quizzes.q: Which sentence is a plan that is already arranged?
options: I meet a friend on Saturday.
I am meeting a friend on Saturday.
I am meet a friend on Saturday.
I meeting a friend on Saturday.
quizzes.a: I am meeting a friend on Saturday.
quizzes.why: An arrangement needs am, is or are and the -ing word. The first is the present simple for routines. The third keeps the plain verb, and the fourth drops am.
After are comes the -ing word: doing. Do and does are present forms with no are, and did is the past.

quizzes.q: Look at that black cloud. It ___ rain.
quizzes.why: A sign you can see takes going to, and going to always needs am, is or are. The first drops is, the third mixes will with going to, and the fourth loses the -ing.

quizzes.q: Which sentence is a guess, and not a decision?
options: I am going to phone the office tomorrow.
We are swapping days next week.
I think it will be warm on Sunday.
She is going to postpone the meeting.
quizzes.a: I think it will be warm on Sunday.
quizzes.why: I think and will mark a guess. The two going to sentences are decisions already made, and the -ing sentence is an arrangement.

quizzes.q: I have decided. I ___ postpone the meeting.
quizzes.why: A decision you have already made takes going to. Possibly and perhaps say you are not sure, and that is the opposite of decided. Am go to is not a form.

quizzes.q: I am going early ___ a seat.
quizzes.why: The reason takes to and a plain verb. For does not go in front of a verb here, to getting adds -ing, and get alone gives no reason.

quizzes.q: Why are you phoning the office?
quizzes.why: A why question is answered with To and a plain verb. For cannot sit in front of a verb. To changing adds -ing. Because needs a whole part with a person in it.
Probably is the strongest of the three sure words. Perhaps and possibly both say it can happen, but you doubt it. Instead is not about being sure at all.
Probably sits between will and the verb. The first puts probably at the end. The second uses is with a plain verb. The third has the word order of a question.

quizzes.q: Which word means small, light rain?
quizzes.why: Drizzle is light rain that falls slowly. Fog is thick cloud on the ground. Thunder is the loud noise in a storm. Frost is white ice on a cold morning.

quizzes.q: Your meeting cannot happen on Monday, so you move it to Friday. What do you do?
quizzes.why: To postpone is to move something to a later time. You forward a message to another person. Spare means extra. You swap when two people exchange with each other.

teacherNotes.note: Every card shows one item done before its practice, every exercise has a key with a score line, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back and a short checklist. Speaking 4 is a two-voice conversation the learner says on their own, both parts, so it needs nobody else. If you are helping, listen to a recording together and point at the checklist rather than correcting mid-sentence.

teacherNotes.type: The one error worth your attention
teacherNotes.note: Two errors carry most of the weight here. The first is the dropped be word: I meeting her on Tuesday, or I going to phone the office. Both patterns are built on am, is and are, and the learner hears them as small, so they disappear first. Ask for the sentence out loud and count three parts. The second is will used for a plan the learner has already decided. Ask one question: did you decide this before now, or are you guessing? Decided takes going to.

No task asks what the learner really does next week, where they work, who they meet or what they pay for. Every diary, day, name and reference in the writing tasks is explicitly made up, and the places are kinds of place with no country and no city. Please keep that wording if you add your own items, and never correct a made-up answer.

Three near neighbours are deliberately absent. There is no if sentence about the future, so If it rains, I will stay at home is not asked for. There is no timetable future, so the train leaves at six is not compared with the -ing arrangement here. And might and may for a small chance are left out; the unit says how sure you are with probably, possibly, perhaps and likely instead. Shall we, learned earlier, appears once in Speaking 4 as a line to say, not as a new pattern.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner, not a marking service. No task here is scored by the tutor alone: every speaking task carries its own checklist and every written task its own countable criteria. The word prompts say plainly where a made-up name or day should be used, and no prompt invites the learner to give the tutor real details about themselves or their week.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what I am doing next week, and name the day.
I can write: It is going to rain. I think it will be fine.
I can say why I am doing something, with to and a plain verb.
I can ask Are you available on Friday? and answer it.
I can say how sure I am: probably, possibly, perhaps, likely.
I can write a short message to move an arrangement.
I can hear whether a speaker is sure or not sure.
I can find what I need in a travel notice.

assignment.title: Next week: arranged, decided and guessed
assignment.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Tap the mic. Talk for one minute about next week. Say two arrangements with am, is or are and an -ing word, one thing you are going to do, one guess about the weather with will, and one sentence with to.
2. Write the message from Writing 4: six sentences, planned first and checked twice.
Every name, day and time can be made up.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written message
